audioChapters.label: Opening — AI is a tool, not a strategy
Mental model: CAC and LTV first

blocks.md:
There are two tribes of marketers in 2026. Tribe A refuses to touch AI; their writers ship four blogs a week, their CAC is ₹847, and they're losing share to Tribe B. Tribe B has wired AI into every workflow; they ship 40 blogs a week, their CAC is ₹1,260, their organic traffic is down 22%, and they're convinced the next prompt will fix it.

Both are wrong, in mirror-image ways. This lesson is about the third path: knowing what your CAC and LTV say *before* you reach for any tool, and only then deciding what AI does and what you do.

blocks.title: Mental model: CAC/LTV first, AI second
blocks.md:
Before any tool, any agency, any prompt: know two numbers.

- **CAC** — what it costs you to acquire one paying customer, *fully loaded* (ad spend + tool costs + your time amortised).
- **LTV** — gross profit you make off that customer over a defined window (12 months for D2C is standard).

If **LTV/CAC < 3**, you don't have a marketing engine. You have a fundraising plan. AI cannot fix that math; it can only run the wrong play faster. Fix the unit economics first; *then* let AI do the volume.

hi-IN.title: Founder ne bola 'AI ad copy lao'
hi-IN.md:
Scene yeh hai. Founder Monday morning meeting mein bola, "yaar, AI use karo, ad copy banao, CAC kam karo." Tu khush. Tuesday tak ChatGPT ne 30 ad copies likh diye. "Buy Now! Limited Time! Don't Miss Out!" Wednesday se launch.

Day 14 — CAC ₹847 se ₹1,640 ho gaya. Founder: "AI kaam nahi kar raha."

Bhai, AI bilkul kaam kar raha hai. AI ne wahi likha jo tu maanga — ad copy. Tu ne yeh nahi maanga ki *positioning* fix karo, *audience* fix karo, *math* check karo. AI ne tujhe wahi diya jo tu ne demand kiya. Aur tu ne demand galat kiya.

en.title: Founder asks AI to lower CAC
en.md:
The founder asks for AI ad copy to lower CAC. By Tuesday you have 30 variants. By day 14, CAC has *risen* from ₹847 to ₹1,640. The founder concludes AI doesn't work.

AI worked exactly as asked. You asked for ad copy. You did not ask whether the positioning, audience, or unit economics were the actual blocker. The AI gave you what you specified. The specification was the problem.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Where the money leaks — 100k impressions → 38 conversions.

blocks.md:
Pick any marketing activity. Ask one question: *which stage of the funnel does this serve?* You will discover that 'we should use AI' is not a strategy — it's a tool reaching for an unspecified problem.

Three stages, in plain English:

- **Top of funnel (TOFU)** — strangers becoming aware. SEO blogs, organic social, podcast ads. High volume, low per-piece consequence. CTR matters more than CAC.
- **Middle of funnel (MOFU)** — interested visitors becoming considerers. Webinars, comparison pages, retargeting ads. Mid volume, mid consequence. CTA quality starts to matter.
- **Bottom of funnel (BOFU)** — considerers becoming buyers. Cart-recovery emails, sales calls, checkout pages. Low volume, high per-piece consequence. One bad line costs a sale.

Different stages have different tolerances for variance. AI's variance is fine at TOFU. It is *expensive* at BOFU.

blocks.title: Translation: 'We should use AI for marketing' → an actually answerable plan

steps.label: Step 1 — Refuse the abstract
steps.body: 'Use AI for marketing' is unanswerable. Say back: 'Which funnel stage are we trying to move, and which metric will we know it by?' Don't move until you have an answer.

steps.label: Step 2 — Pick the stage
steps.body: Founder says: 'Lower CAC.' That's BOFU territory (or a positioning fix; see Step 4). Now we know what we're optimising.

steps.label: Step 3 — Pick the metric
steps.body: CAC has many cousins: blended CAC, paid CAC, CAC by channel, CAC by cohort. Pick one and write it down: 'Paid CAC for new D2C buyers acquired this month.'

steps.label: Step 4 — Diagnose before tooling
steps.body: Is the math broken (LTV/CAC < 3)? AI won't fix that. Is the creative tired? AI can help. Is the audience wrong? AI can help find a better one. Different diagnosis, different tool.

steps.label: Step 5 — Pick the AI ratio
steps.body: TOFU drafts at 80% AI, voice review human. BOFU emails 50/50, cart-recovery copy human-led. Crisis PR — human only. The ratio comes from the diagnosis, not the tool catalogue.

blocks.prompt: Your founder says, 'we should use AI to lower CAC by 30% this quarter.' What is the *first* thing you ask before reaching for a tool?

choices.label: What's our current LTV, and what's our LTV/CAC ratio?
choices.explain: Right. If LTV/CAC < 3, lowering CAC alone is rearranging deck chairs. Diagnose the math first.

choices.label: Which AI tool should we buy?
choices.explain: Tools-first is the named trap. The diagnosis tells you what tool you need; not the other way around.

choices.label: How many blog posts can we ship?
choices.explain: Volume question. Doesn't tell you whether more volume helps.

choices.label: Should we hire an agency?
choices.explain: Org question. Comes after diagnosis, not before.

hi-IN.title: Meesho catalog wala lesson
hi-IN.md:
Meesho ke catalog mein ek pattern hai: top-of-funnel mein 5,000 product photos, sab AI-generated background, sab fine. Lekin checkout page ka copy? Bhai, woh 100% human-written hai. "COD available, 7-day return, free shipping over ₹499" — ek bhi AI-tweak nahi.

Kyun? Kyunki 5,000 catalog photos mein se 1 dud chalega. Checkout copy mein ek bhi galti — order drop ho gaya. Stakes ka ratio yahaan dikhta hai.

en.title: Meesho's quiet AI/human split
en.md: Meesho runs thousands of AI-generated product photos at the top of the funnel and barely-touched human-written copy at checkout. The reasoning is the same: variance at TOFU is absorbed by volume; variance at BOFU is paid for in lost orders.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · 1% lift × 5 steps = 5% lift? — it compounds, badly.

blocks.md:
Once you can name the stage, the AI question becomes specific instead of philosophical. Here is the rule of thumb that holds across D2C, SaaS, and edtech: **as the stakes per piece rise, the human ratio rises with them.**

A crisp number from a Pune D2C wellness brand scaling to Tier-2 cities last March: when they shifted ad-creative drafting from 100% human to 80% AI / 20% human review, output went 4x and CAC moved from ₹920 to ₹910 (within noise). When they tried the same shift on cart-abandonment emails, CAC moved from ₹920 to ₹1,140 — the AI emails sounded plausible but failed the brand-voice anchor at the moment users were closest to deciding. They reverted BOFU to human-led within two weeks.

The lesson is not that AI is bad at writing. The lesson is that *where you put it in the funnel* changes whether it pays you back.

coach.name: Growth-Lead Gauri
coach.role: D2C veteran, 11 years across Mumbai and Bengaluru, has fired three agencies and one founder

intro: Hi. Gauri here. We have ten minutes; let's not waste them.
I'm going to throw five real-world asks at you. You tell me — is this a job for **AI 80%**, **Human 80%**, or **diagnose first** (we don't have enough info)?
There's no shame in 'diagnose first'. That's usually the right answer. People skip it because it feels lazy. It's actually the move.

scenarios.situation: Founder: 'Generate 200 SEO meta descriptions for our product catalogue this week.'
scenarios.explain: Pure TOFU, high volume, low per-piece stakes. Classic AI 80%. A human voice-checks a sample and ships.

scenarios.situation: Performance marketer: 'Rewrite our cart-abandonment email; CAC is up 18% this month.'
scenarios.explain: Don't reach for AI yet. Why is CAC up? New audience? Stockouts? Pricing change? The email may be fine; the upstream may not be. Diagnose, then act.

scenarios.situation: PR head: 'We just had a product recall; help me write the public statement by 8pm.'
scenarios.explain: Crisis PR is the brand 20%. AI default-frames toward generic empathy that reads hollow. Human writes; AI may copy-edit.

scenarios.situation: Junior: 'Should I use AI to translate our Hindi blog to Marathi for the Pune launch?'
scenarios.explain: Maybe. Marathi has tonal nuances that LLMs handle inconsistently in 2026; output needs a Marathi-speaking review pass. So: AI draft + human review = a 50/50, not a clean AI 80%. Worth diagnosing.

scenarios.situation: Founder: 'Use AI to write 1,000 personalised birthday emails to our top customers.'
scenarios.explain: Mid volume, low per-piece stakes (a missed birthday email is a non-event), heavy templating. AI 80% with a brand-voice template lock.

scenarios.situation: CMO: 'Refresh the homepage hero copy for the Q3 launch.'
scenarios.explain: One asset, top of every visit, sets brand tone. The 20% that's worth a human's full attention.

blocks.title: The classic trap: AI tactics without metrics
blocks.md:
The single most common failure mode in 2026: someone writes 'AI ad copy' on a Q-plan, ships 200 variants, and reports 'we shipped 200 variants' as if shipping were the goal.

**Shipping is not a metric.** CAC, ROAS, payback period, retention — those are metrics. If your AI plan does not say 'we expect CAC to move from X to Y by date Z, and if it doesn't, we will do A', you have an *activity plan* dressed as a strategy. The tell: the plan is full of tool names and short on numbers.

blocks.prompt: Drag these into the right order — the diagnostic sequence before any AI marketing decision.

items.label: Compute LTV/CAC for the relevant cohort
items.detail: Numbers first; without them, every later choice is unanchored.

items.label: Identify which funnel stage the metric lives at
items.detail: Top, middle, or bottom changes everything that follows.

items.label: Decide whether the issue is math, audience, creative, or product
items.detail: Each diagnosis points to a different tool.

items.label: Pick the AI ratio for that stage and that diagnosis
items.detail: TOFU + creative-tired = AI heavy. BOFU + audience-wrong = human-led with AI assists.

items.label: Set a kill criterion before launch
items.detail: If you can't say 'we'd kill this at X', you can't honestly run it.

blocks.hint: Math, then stage, then diagnosis, then ratio, then criterion. Resist the urge to pick the tool first.

blocks.instruction:
Take this real founder ask and rewrite it as an answerable diagnostic question.

**Founder ask:** "Use AI to grow our marketing 5x this quarter."

Write three numbered diagnostic questions you'd ask before saying anything else. Then write the one-sentence reply you'd send back to the founder by end of day.
blocks.expected:
Diagnostic questions:
1. What's our current LTV/CAC ratio, and which channel is currently weakest on payback?
2. Of our current marketing spend, what fraction goes to top-of-funnel, mid, and bottom — and which stage are we trying to grow 5x?
3. Is '5x' on output (volume), on revenue, or on a specific metric like new-customer acquisitions?

Reply to founder:
'Happy to scope this. Quick check first — is the 5x on revenue, on output, or on a stage-specific metric like new acquisitions? The answer changes the AI ratio I'd recommend by a lot. I'll have a numbered plan in your inbox by Friday once we align on that one number.'

blocks.prompt: A SaaS founder shows you these numbers: CAC ₹4,200, 12-month LTV ₹6,100, AI tools budget approved. What is the *most defensible* opening recommendation?

choices.label: Don't scale paid acquisition; LTV/CAC is 1.45 — fix LTV (retention, expansion, pricing) before adding AI volume.
choices.explain: Right. Adding AI to a broken-math channel just buys revenue at near-cost faster. Fix LTV first.

choices.label: Use AI to lower CAC by 30%; that fixes the ratio.
choices.explain: Tempting, but a 30% CAC drop on its own only moves the ratio to 2.06 — still under the 3x line. AI is buying you a smaller hole, not a profitable one.

choices.label: Generate 50 AI-written blogs for SEO this month.
choices.explain: Volume play with no link to the diagnosis. Will likely worsen the math by adding tooling spend without retention impact.

choices.label: Hire two more performance marketers.
choices.explain: Adds CAC inputs (overhead) to a CAC problem. Wrong direction.

hi-IN.title: Mummy-aunty test for marketing math
hi-IN.md:
Mummy ke saath baith ke samjha. "Ek customer banane mein ₹847 lagta hai. Ek customer humein ₹4,200 deta hai over a year."

Mummy: "Toh achha business hai."

Doosra scenario. "Ek customer ₹4,200 mein banata hu. Mujhe ₹6,100 milta hai."

Mummy: "Beta, itna mehnat karke itna kam? Aur isme tax bhi hoga. Yeh business kya kar raha hai?"

Mummy-aunty test paas. LTV/CAC < 3 means even your mom thinks something's off.

en.title: The mom test for unit economics
en.md: Explain your CAC and LTV to someone with no marketing vocabulary. If they say 'that doesn't sound like a business', you don't have a marketing problem; you have a fundamentals problem. AI cannot rescue fundamentals.

blocks.title: Field Notes: ROAS unchanged, CAC up 14%
blocks.source: Anonymous founder of a Pune skincare D2C, 12-person team
blocks.story:
Q1 2026 was our 'AI-powered marketing' quarter. We added Jasper for ads copy, Mailchimp's AI for email subject lines, an AI chatbot, AI-personalized product recs, AI-driven creative generation. Marketing lead spent 14 weeks integrating tools. Investor decks were thrilling.

Quarter close: ROAS unchanged from Q4. CAC up 14%. The AI tactics added cost on the input side (subscriptions ₹4.2 lakh/quarter) and noise on the output side (3% of ad copy got flagged for brand-tone issues, ate up review cycles).

**The mistake was the framing.** I'd told my team 'use AI for everything.' I should have told them 'pin the metric first, then ask what AI move moves IT.' The metric we cared about was return on D7 (D7 retention × first-purchase margin). None of our AI tactics targeted D7 retention. We were AI-decorating the funnel without moving anything.
blocks.takeaway: AI tactics without a pinned metric inflate cost without moving outcome. Always reverse: metric first, AI move second.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: ₹40L for AI marketing
blocks.setup: Sneha just got handed ₹40 lakh for Q2 marketing. Her founder said 'use AI to do the work of 5 people.' Her CMO sent her a list of 14 AI tools to try. Sneha has 10 minutes to decide where to start.

stages.prompt: Sneha's instinct: split ₹40L across the top 7 AI tools. What does Vrinda say?

options.label: Yes — 'AI everywhere' is the directive.
options.explain: Same trap as the Pune skincare brand. Multiplies cost without moving any single outcome.

options.label: Pin the north-star metric first. Then pick the 1-2 AI moves that target it.
options.explain: Right. 'Use AI for everything' becomes 'use AI to move metric Z by ≥X% by Date Y'.

options.label: Split across 14 tools to maximize coverage.
options.explain: Most decorative possible move. Each tool gets ₹2.8L; none gets shipped properly.

stages.prompt: Sneha picks D7 retention × first-purchase margin as her north star. Which AI move targets it best?

options.label: AI-personalized post-purchase email sequence (segments-based, A/B tested) targeting day-7 re-engagement.
options.explain: Right. Direct lever on D7 retention. Segments-based avoids creepiness; A/B testing keeps it honest.

options.label: AI-generated brand awareness ads (top-of-funnel).
options.explain: Decorative for D7 retention; ToF doesn't move retention metrics.

options.label: AI chatbot on the website.
options.explain: Mid-funnel. Useful but doesn't directly target D7 retention.

options.label: AI-generated social media content for engagement.
options.explain: Vanity-metric trap.

stages.prompt: Day 14 of the campaign. D7 retention up 6%. CAC unchanged. ROAS up 8%. CMO says 'apply AI everywhere now!'

options.label: Hold the line. Validate at day 30 with another 14-day cycle. Don't expand until D7 lift is replicated.
options.explain: Right. 14-day signal is encouraging; not a cleared replication. Apply discipline.

options.label: Expand immediately to all funnel stages.
options.explain: Same Q1 mistake one quarter later. Validation first, then expansion.

options.label: Kill the campaign because CAC didn't move.
options.explain: Wrong metric. The campaign targeted D7 retention, not CAC.

outcomes.perfect: Sneha walks out with a clean experiment + a discipline she'll reuse for Q3 and Q4. Founder asks for AI strategy doc; Sneha shares the 1-page.
outcomes.good: Solid signal. The AI-everywhere instinct held off this time; needs reinforcement on the next campaign.
outcomes.learn: Re-read the metric-first section. AI without a pinned outcome is decoration, not strategy.

points: If LTV/CAC is under 3, you don't have a marketing engine — you have a fundraising plan, and AI cannot rescue the math.
'Use AI for marketing' is not a strategy; it's a tool reaching for an unspecified problem.
The funnel-stage lens decides everything: TOFU absorbs AI variance, BOFU pays for it in lost sales.
Diagnose before tooling: math, audience, creative, or product — each points to a different AI ratio.
If your AI plan has no 'we will move metric X to Y by date Z, or do A', you have an activity plan, not a strategy.

lessons.title: AI-Powered Content Pipeline
lessons.subtitle: Brief, draft, review, ship — and where AI fits in each

audioChapters.label: Mental model: brief → draft → review → ship

blocks.md:
Most teams adopt AI for content the same way: turn it on, ship 10x volume, watch traffic die six months later, blame Google. The pattern has a name now — *AI-generated SEO slop* — and the search engines have been training on it for two years. They are very good at spotting it.

The answer is not to abandon AI. It's to stop treating AI as a content factory and start treating it as one stage in a four-stage pipeline. The pipeline is the protection. Without it, you ship slop. With it, you ship 4x volume at the same quality, which is the actual win.

blocks.title: Mental model: brief → draft → review → ship
blocks.md:
Every piece of content should pass through four stages, in order, no skipping.

1. **Brief** — A human writes what we are saying, to whom, in whose voice, and why now. *This is the unskippable step.* If the brief is weak, every downstream stage is downstream of weak.
2. **Draft** — AI does the heavy lifting here. This is the 80%.
3. **Review** — The 3-pass review (we'll get to it). This is what stops slop from shipping.
4. **Ship** — A human owns the final yes. Not a Slack thread, not a 'looks fine'. A name.

hi-IN.title: Agency ne bola '100 articles in a week'
hi-IN.md:
Pune ki ek edtech ne agency hire ki. Pitch tha: "AI use karke 100 SEO articles in a week, ranking guaranteed." Founder bola, "deal."

Week 1 — 100 articles live. Founder Slack pe bragging.
Week 8 — 100 articles still live. Traffic same.
Week 12 — Google ne update mara. Site-wide ranking 47% gir gayi. Helpful Content Update ka classic case.

Founder ne agency ko gaali di. Lekin sach yeh hai — agency ne wahi delivered jo promise tha. Volume. Brief koi nahi tha. Voice koi nahi thi. Review koi nahi thi. Sirf draft tha, multiplied by 100. Slop, by design.

en.title: The 100-articles-a-week trap
en.md: A Pune edtech bought an agency package promising '100 SEO articles per week, ranking guaranteed in 90 days, fully AI'. Three months in, a search algorithm update dropped site rankings 47%. The agency had delivered exactly what was promised. Volume without brief, voice, or review is a slop machine. The metric the agency optimised for was the wrong metric.

blocks.md:
AI defaults to a tone called *generic LinkedIn earnest*. You can spot it in three sentences: short paragraphs, lots of em-dashes, em-dashes used as commas, vague affirmations, and a closing call-to-action that says 'embrace the journey'. Two of your competitors are shipping it right now. Your customers cannot tell their content apart from yours when you let AI run unanchored.

The fix is not 'add a style guide PDF to the prompt'. The fix is the **brand-voice anchor**: a 200-300 word document with three things — *do say*, *don't say*, and *three short sample paragraphs in the voice we actually have*. You hand it to AI on every prompt. You hand it to every reviewer. The anchor is what stops drift.

A real anchor for a Mumbai D2C beauty brand we worked with last quarter:

- *Do say:* 'six-week routine', 'because skin barriers don't read marketing', 'this is for people who tried five things already'.
- *Don't say:* 'unlock your glow', 'embrace your inner beauty', 'transform your journey'.
- Three sample paragraphs from their best-performing 2025 emails attached.

Result: AI drafts went from 'rejectable on voice' to 'shippable with light copy-edit' in a week.

steps.label: Step 1 — Find your three voice anchors
steps.body: Open the three highest-performing pieces of content from the last 12 months. Highlight the lines a customer would quote. Those are your voice anchors. Real sentences, not vibes.

steps.label: Step 2 — Write a Do/Don't list
steps.body: From those highlights, extract patterns. 'Do say: specific timeframes, ratio numbers, named customer types.' 'Don't say: aspirational verbs without a noun behind them, journey metaphors, glow.'

steps.label: Step 3 — Attach 3 full sample paragraphs
steps.body: Tell AI: 'Write in the voice of these three paragraphs.' Paste them. AI is a pattern-matcher; it pattern-matches what you give it.

steps.label: Step 4 — Lock it in the system prompt
steps.body: Don't paste the anchor into every chat. Wire it into your tooling — Notion AI, Claude project, whatever you use. The anchor should be persistent infrastructure, not a per-task copy-paste.

steps.label: Step 5 — Audit drift monthly
steps.body: Take 5 random pieces shipped this month. Compare to anchor. Score each on a 1-5 voice match. If average drops below 4, refresh the samples.

choices.label: Attach 3 high-performing real paragraphs from your archives as voice samples in the system prompt.
choices.explain: Right. Pattern-match in beats abstraction every time. Real paragraphs > adjectives.

choices.explain: Adjectives like 'witty' and 'engaging' are exactly what AI was trained on as filler. They make output worse, not better.

choices.explain: Tool swap won't fix a brief problem. The same generic output appears across all major models when un-anchored.

choices.label: Increase output volume to 'find the gems'.
choices.explain: Volume amplifies the problem; you ship more generic content faster.

hi-IN.title: Naani's recipe vs Swiggy recipe
hi-IN.md:
Naani ki dal makhani ka recipe likhwao. "Beta, pehle kasoori methi haath se mal ke daalo, warna kadwa lagega. Tomato pakka pakao, varna khatta. Cream end mein, varna phat jayegi."

Swiggy ke menu pe likha hai: "Authentic, creamy, rich, indulgent."

Dono dal makhani hai. Ek mein **specifics** hai. Doosre mein **adjectives** hai. AI default Swiggy-mode mein likhta hai. Tu use Naani-mode mein dhakelta hai sample paragraphs deke.

en.title: Specifics over adjectives
en.md: Your grandmother's recipe says 'crush the kasoori methi between your palms or it tastes bitter'. The food-app menu says 'authentic, creamy, rich, indulgent'. Both describe the same dish. One has specifics; the other has adjectives. AI defaults to adjective-mode; samples push it to specifics-mode.

blocks.md:
Once a draft exists, three passes — in order, by name. Each pass has one job. None of them is 'general edit'.

1. **Voice pass** — Does this sound like our brand or like generic ChatGPT? You read it out loud; if your CMO would not say this sentence, it gets a strike.
2. **Fact pass** — Is every claim, statistic, and product detail correct? AI confidently invents stats. The 2024 average ad-spend numbers it 'cites' are often hallucinated. Verify.
3. **Slop pass** — Does this earn its length? Are there filler paragraphs whose removal nobody would notice? Cut them. The shortest version that still works wins.

In that order, because catching a voice problem after fact-checking is wasted fact-checking. And catching slop before voice means you've cut the wrong things.

coach.name: Growth-Lead Gauri
coach.role: D2C veteran, has rejected 1,400 drafts in the last 18 months and kept score

intro: Back. We do reviews differently here. I'll show you 6 lines from real AI drafts.
Tell me which pass would catch each: **Voice**, **Fact**, or **Slop** (filler that earns nothing).
If a line has multiple problems, pick the *first* pass that catches it. Order matters.

scenarios.situation: 'Embrace your skincare journey with our scientifically-engineered formulations designed for the modern Indian woman.'
scenarios.explain: Pure generic-LinkedIn-earnest. 'Embrace', 'journey', 'scientifically-engineered', 'modern Indian woman' — every phrase is interchangeable with three competitors'. Voice pass kills it.

scenarios.situation: 'A 2024 Nielsen study found that 73% of Indian D2C buyers prefer AI-personalised emails.' (No such study exists.)
scenarios.explain: Hallucinated statistic. Sounds plausible; isn't real. Fact pass catches it before it ships and embarrasses you in court.

scenarios.situation: 'In today's fast-paced digital landscape, brands must navigate an evolving consumer ecosystem.'
scenarios.explain: Voice pass *could* kill it; it's also a filler sentence whose removal nobody would notice. The slop pass is the cleaner kill.

scenarios.situation: 'Our new serum reduces fine lines in 7 days, backed by a 200-person clinical trial.' (Trial was 40 people, results were 14 days, not 7.)
scenarios.explain: Half-true. Worse than fully invented; sounds defensible until someone checks. Fact pass.

scenarios.situation: 'In conclusion, content marketing is more important than ever in 2026.'
scenarios.explain: The 'in conclusion' tell. Adds zero. Cut and the piece is stronger.

scenarios.situation: 'Hey gorgeous! Ready to glow up your weekend? Our drop is HERE!' — for a brand whose voice is dry and clinical.
scenarios.explain: Mismatch with the brand-voice anchor. Voice pass.

blocks.title: The classic trap: AI-generated SEO slop
blocks.md:
The slop pattern: high volume + no voice anchor + no fact pass + 'rank-first, value-second'. Search engines have been trained on this exact signature for two years; they spot it within weeks of indexing.

The symptom is delayed: traffic looks fine for 4-8 weeks, then drops 20-50% after the next core update. The damage is sticky — recovering site-wide trust takes 3-6 months of *removing* low-quality pages and shipping fewer, better ones.

The fix is upstream. Don't ship slop in the first place. The 3-pass review is not optional bureaucracy; it's the cheapest insurance you have.

blocks.instruction:
Below is a real AI-drafted opening paragraph for a D2C wellness brand:

'In today's rapidly evolving wellness landscape, modern Indian consumers are increasingly seeking personalised, holistic solutions that align with their unique lifestyle journeys. Our new ashwagandha-based formulation has been scientifically engineered to deliver transformative results, harnessing the power of ancient Ayurvedic wisdom backed by cutting-edge research.'

Apply the 3-pass review. For each pass, write what you'd flag. Then write the rewritten version that survives all three.
blocks.expected:
Voice pass: every phrase is generic. 'Today's rapidly evolving', 'modern Indian consumers', 'personalised holistic solutions', 'transformative results', 'cutting-edge research' — all interchangeable filler. Strike.

Fact pass: 'scientifically engineered' has no specific study cited. 'Cutting-edge research' has no source. Both unverifiable. Strike.

Slop pass: of 60 words, maybe 8 carry information (ashwagandha, Ayurvedic, formulation). 52 words of vapor. Strike.

Rewrite (a survivable version, in a dry voice with specifics):
'We made a new ashwagandha capsule. Single-ingredient, 600mg, third-party tested for heavy metals (certificate on the page). It targets one thing: cortisol-driven sleep loss. If your problem is 'wired but tired at 11pm', it's worth six weeks. If not, save your money.'

blocks.prompt: You inherit a content backlog of 200 AI-drafted blog posts that haven't shipped. Time and budget allow you to ship only 60. Which culling rule survives the 3-pass logic?

choices.label: Cut the 80 with the weakest voice match to your anchor first.
choices.explain: Right. Voice failures are the most expensive long-term — they erode brand recognition. Cut these first.

choices.label: Cut the 30 with unverifiable claims; reposition as opinion pieces only if the opinion has earned its place.
choices.explain: Right. Fact-pass failures are legal risk and credibility risk. Cull aggressively.

choices.label: Ship the longest 60; length signals depth.
choices.explain: Length is uncorrelated with quality and is the slop pattern in disguise. Don't reward word count.

choices.label: Ship all 200 — let the audience decide.
choices.explain: The audience decides via traffic loss after the next algorithm update. Volume-cide is the loud version of this mistake.

hi-IN.title: Mummy ka 'isme namak kam hai' test
hi-IN.md:
Mummy taste karti hai. "Beta, kuch missing hai." Tu adjective add karta hai — "flavorful, rich, savory". Mummy: "Namak daal."

Voice pass yahi hai. Tujhe content padh ke ek chhota sa missing-piece dikhna chahiye. Adjective daalna easy hai. Specifics daalna mehnat hai. Mummy hamesha specifics maangti hai.

en.title: The 'something's missing' test
en.md: Your mom tastes the dish, says 'something's missing'. You can either add adjectives ('rich, savoury, flavourful') or salt. The voice pass works the same way. Filler is the adjectives. Specificity is the salt.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 100 articles, ranking gone in 21 days
blocks.source: Anonymous SEO consultant at a Mumbai content agency
blocks.story:
Client asked us to publish 100 articles in 7 days. Brief: 'use AI to scale.' We did. 100 AI-drafted, lightly-edited blog posts went live across two weeks.

Week 3 of week-3: Google's spam-content update hit. **Domain authority dropped from 47 to 11.** 73 of the 100 articles got de-indexed. Organic traffic fell 84%. Client lost ~₹30 lakh in pipeline that quarter.

The 27 surviving articles? They were the ones we had a writer rewrite top-to-bottom — i.e., the ones where AI was a starter draft, not the shipped artifact. The agency kept the client by spending Q4 doing content cleanup: deleting 73, rebuilding 47 with full human craft. We charged the client extra. Could have charged less and shipped 12 great articles to begin with.
blocks.takeaway: AI-as-shipped-artifact loses to AI-as-draft + human craft. Volume is a vanity metric; rankings live or die on craft.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: 100 articles or 12?

options.explain: Right. Volume is the vanity; craft is the asset. Re-frame the budget around outcome, not output count.

options.label: Approve the 100 plan; ship at scale.
options.explain: Same Mumbai agency story plays out. Ranking risk is unbounded.

options.label: Reject content entirely.
options.explain: Overcorrection. Content with craft is still leverage; just not at 100/month volumes.

options.explain: Evidence-backed framing. Founder updates priors.

options.label: 'Trust me, 100 is bad.'
options.explain: Founder doesn't update on assertion. Need evidence.

options.label: 'Other brands are wrong.'
options.explain: Doesn't help. Frame the risk in $ and rankings, not opinions.

options.label: Brief (with brand voice anchor) → AI draft → human structure edit → human voice edit → SEO review → ship. 5 stages.
options.explain: Right. Each stage adds craft. The brand voice anchor is what AI cannot replicate without 3 sample posts.

options.label: AI draft → ship.
options.explain: Same de-indexing risk; just 12 articles instead of 100.

options.label: AI draft → quick proofread → ship.
options.explain: Single human gate insufficient. Three gates (structure, voice, SEO) is the discipline.

outcomes.learn: Re-read the de-indexing case. Volume without craft is a ranking risk, not an asset.

lessons.title: Ads, A/B Tests, and the Statistical Reality
lessons.subtitle: Why your day-2 'winner' is almost always noise

audioChapters.label: Mental model: minimum sample size > 'we have a winner'

blocks.md:
Day 2 of an A/B test. Variant B is showing a 14% lift in click-through rate. Your boss messages the team channel: 'B is the winner — let's roll out!' Twelve people react with thumbs-ups. Nobody asks how many impressions B has had.

If you have ever shipped this scene, you have spent money to learn that random variance feels exactly like a real result. The whole point of statistical thinking in marketing is to refuse the feeling. The cost of the refusal is small. The cost of skipping it is the entire reason your last six 'winning' campaigns underperformed at scale.

blocks.title: Mental model: sample size is the unit, not days
blocks.md:
Marketing teams measure experiments in *days* because the dashboard shows days. Statistics measures experiments in *sample size*. They are not the same.

- A 7-day test on a low-traffic campaign can have less data than a 1-day test on a high-traffic one.
- A 'big' lift (14%) on a small sample (1,200) tells you almost nothing.
- A 'small' lift (3%) on a large sample (4,700) can be a real, durable signal.

The rule: **before you launch, compute the minimum sample size you need. Until you hit it, you have no conclusion.** This is the no-conclusion-yet rule. It saves more money than any AI tool ever will.

hi-IN.title: Founder ne day 2 mein 'winner' declare kar diya
hi-IN.md:
Bengaluru SaaS, last March. Founder ne A/B test launch kara — naya CTA vs purana. Day 2, naye CTA mein 18% lift. Founder ne Slack pe announce kara: "NEW CTA WINS. ROLLING OUT."

Day 14 — full rollout ke baad — actual conversion *down 4%*. Founder confused. Performance marketer ne dekha — day 2 wala sample tha 800 impressions per variant. Statistical noise band of ±22%. 18% lift was inside the noise.

Founder bola, "data ne galat bola." Bhai, data ne kuch nahi bola. Tu ne sample size dekha hi nahi.

en.title: Day 2 winner, day 14 loser
en.md: A Bengaluru SaaS declared a CTA winner on day 2 with an 18% lift on 800 impressions per variant. The noise band on that sample was ±22%. The 'lift' was inside the noise. Two weeks after rolling out, conversions were *down* 4%. The founder said 'the data lied'. The data said nothing. The sample size was the part that hadn't shown up yet.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · 7 variants, 7 segments, one afternoon — matrix populating.

blocks.md:
The no-conclusion-yet rule is two sentences:

1. Before launch, compute the minimum sample size needed to detect the *minimum lift you'd act on*, with 80% statistical power and 95% confidence.
2. Until you hit that sample size, the answer to 'who's winning?' is 'no conclusion yet'. Not 'A is leading'. Not 'B looks promising'. *No conclusion yet.*

The math is not optional, but it is also not hard. For a baseline conversion rate of 4% and a minimum detectable lift of 5%, you need roughly **4,700 impressions per variant** to declare a winner with 95% confidence and 80% power. Higher base rates need fewer impressions; smaller lifts need more.

A real number: a Pune D2C wellness brand running Meta ads at 800 impressions per variant per day needs *six days minimum* before any A/B test result is honest. Anything shorter is the team performing rigour without doing it. The dashboard does not tell you this; you have to write it down before launching.

blocks.title: Translation: 'Let's A/B test the new ad' → an honest experiment plan

steps.label: Step 1 — Decide what would matter
steps.body: Ask: 'What lift would change our decision?' If a 1% lift wouldn't change anything, don't run a test that needs 100k+ impressions to detect it. Pick the lift you'd act on; usually 5-10%.

steps.label: Step 2 — Compute the sample size
steps.body: For your baseline rate and minimum detectable lift, get the per-variant sample size. Free calculators do this in 30 seconds. Write the number down where the team can see it.

steps.label: Step 3 — Estimate test duration honestly
steps.body: Sample size needed / daily impressions per variant = honest minimum days. If that exceeds your patience, either pick a bigger lift to detect, or run the test on a higher-traffic asset.

steps.label: Step 4 — Pre-register the kill criteria
steps.body: Write down: 'We will not declare a winner before day X. If by day X the lift is < 3%, we'll continue running A.' This is the no-conclusion-yet rule, on paper, before launch.

steps.label: Step 5 — On the date, look at the data and act
steps.body: Not before. Not after seeing day-2 numbers. The point of pre-registration is to bind your future self.

blocks.prompt: Your campaign delivers 600 impressions per variant per day. You compute that to detect a 5% lift, you need 4,700 per variant. Your boss wants a winner declared by Friday (4 days from launch). The honest answer is:

choices.label: Tell the boss: minimum honest test is ~8 days; declaring on Friday is theatre. Either extend the timeline or pick a bigger lift threshold (10%, ~1,200 impressions).
choices.explain: Right. The no-conclusion-yet rule. Honest math, presented as options, lets the boss choose without lying about what's possible.

choices.label: Run anyway and declare the leading variant on Friday.
choices.explain: This is the failure mode the rule was designed to prevent.

choices.label: Use AI to estimate what the result *would* be at full sample size.
choices.explain: Tool-substitution for math doesn't work; the AI's prediction inherits the same noise.

choices.label: Stop running A/B tests; they're too slow.
choices.explain: Throwing out the rigour throws out the only mechanism that distinguishes lift from noise.

hi-IN.title: Cricket scoreboard ka analogy
hi-IN.md:
T20 match. India ne 4 overs mein 60 run banaye. Commentator bola, "India is on track for 360." Tu hassi.

Kyun? Kyunki 4 overs ka data full match predict nahi karta. Variance bahut zyada hai shuru mein.

A/B test bhi waisa hi hai. Day 2 ka data full campaign nahi predict karta. Tu cricket mein commentator par hass-ta hai. A/B test mein khud ban-ta hai.

en.title: The 4-over projection
en.md: When a cricket commentator says 'on track for 360' after 4 overs, you laugh. Early data has huge variance; the projection is meaningless. A/B tests work the same way. Day 2 'projections' have the same problem; the only difference is that nobody laughs at marketing dashboards.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Same offer, three voices — voice changes, claim stays.

blocks.md:
The second move is a habit of seeing. Every time you look at a 'lift' number, ask: *what's the noise band?* If the lift is inside the noise band, the result is statistically indistinguishable from chance — even if the dashboard makes it look heroic.

The rough heuristic that gets you 80% of the way there:

- For a CTR baseline around 2-5%, the 95% noise band at sample size N is roughly ±2 × √(p(1-p)/N) × 100%.
- At N=1,000, baseline 4%: noise band ±1.2 percentage points, or roughly ±30% of the base rate.
- At N=5,000, same baseline: noise band ±0.55pp, roughly ±14%.
- At N=20,000: noise band ±0.27pp, roughly ±7%.

So: at 1,000 impressions, anything under a 30% lift is noise. At 5,000, anything under 14%. At 20,000, anything under 7%. The 14% lift on 1,200 impressions that started this lesson? Inside the noise band. The team that high-fived was applauding randomness.

coach.name: Growth-Lead Gauri
coach.role: D2C veteran, has buried six campaigns that 'won' on noise

intro: Statistical reality time. I'll throw five A/B test situations at you.
Tell me: is this a **real lift**, **inside noise**, or **need more data** (sample isn't yet enough to call it)?
These are real numbers from real campaigns. Most teams get them wrong — the bias is always toward declaring winners. Resist it.

scenarios.situation: Day 2. Variant B shows +14% CTR over A. n = 1,200 per variant. Baseline 4%.
scenarios.explain: At n=1,200 the noise band is roughly ±28% of the base rate. A 14% lift sits comfortably inside. Looks dramatic; isn't real.

scenarios.situation: Day 8. Variant B shows +6% CTR over A. n = 22,000 per variant. Baseline 4%.
scenarios.explain: At n=22k the noise band is roughly ±7%. A 6% lift is just outside it — borderline real, and worth a confirmation run, but it's a defensible call.

scenarios.situation: Day 4. Variant B shows +8% CTR over A. n = 3,500 per variant. Baseline 4%.
scenarios.explain: At n=3,500 noise is ±17%. The 8% sits inside the band. You'd need closer to n=8,000 to call it. Wait, don't kill — keep running.

scenarios.situation: Day 14. Variant B shows +35% CTR over A. n = 800 per variant. (Low-volume B2B campaign.)
scenarios.explain: Day count is irrelevant; sample size is the unit. At n=800 the noise band is enormous (~35%). A 35% lift is right at the edge. Could be real, but the test cannot honestly distinguish lift from noise at this sample.

scenarios.situation: Day 10. Variant B shows +1% CTR over A. n = 50,000 per variant. Baseline 4%.
scenarios.explain: At n=50k the noise band shrinks to ±4-5%. A 1% lift is *not* outside noise either. But this is the type of test where nothing wins — the variants are basically equivalent. Honest answer: keep the simpler one.

scenarios.situation: Day 6. Variant B shows +9% CTR over A. n = 5,200 per variant. Baseline 4%.
scenarios.explain: At n=5,200 the noise band is ~14%. 9% is inside it; barely. Borderline — most teams call this 'real' and ship. Honest framing: weak signal, would re-confirm with another 7 days.

blocks.title: The classic trap: declared winner at day 2, still noise
blocks.md:
The trap is structural, not personal. Dashboards show daily numbers; daily numbers feel meaningful; meaningful-feeling numbers get acted on. The cure is a habit, not a tool.

The habit: every time someone says 'B is winning', your reflex sentence is **'how many impressions, and what's the noise band?'** If they can't answer both, the answer to 'is B winning?' is no conclusion yet. Repeat this in three meetings and the team starts saying it for you.

items.label: Define the minimum lift that would change a decision
items.detail: 1%? 5%? 10%? Pick the smallest delta that would actually move you to ship the variant.

items.label: Compute the sample size needed for that lift
items.detail: Use a power calculator. 30 seconds.

items.label: Estimate honest test duration
items.detail: Sample size / daily impressions per variant. If too long, escalate or rescope.

blocks.hint: Lift you'd act on → sample size → duration → write down the rule → launch → decide on the date.

blocks.instruction:
You're running Meta ads for an Indore-based D2C brand. Baseline CTR is 3.5%. Daily impressions per variant: 1,400. You want to detect a 7% lift. Compute:

1. Approximate sample size needed per variant.
2. Honest minimum test duration in days.
3. A one-paragraph 'pre-registration' note you'd email the team before launch — covering the lift threshold, the duration, and what you'll do if the test ends inconclusive.
blocks.expected:
1. Sample size: For baseline 3.5% and 7% relative lift (i.e. detecting +0.245pp), at 80% power and 95% confidence you need approximately 8,500-9,000 impressions per variant.

2. Honest duration: 9,000 / 1,400 ≈ 6.4 days, so seven full days minimum.

3. Pre-registration note:
'Team, launching the cart-recovery email A/B test tomorrow. Variant A = current control; Variant B = new subject line + opening. We've calculated that detecting a 7% relative lift with 95% confidence and 80% power requires ~9,000 impressions per variant; at our current 1,400/day, that's seven days. We will NOT declare a winner before day 7. If by day 7 the lift is below 7% in either direction, our default is to keep variant A (the simpler one) and treat the test as inconclusive. If between 7-15%, we extend by another 3 days for confirmation. If above 15%, we ship. No mid-test rollouts. — [Your Name]'

blocks.prompt: You're presenting test results to a non-technical founder. Which of these are honest framings? (pick two)

choices.label: 'At our current sample size, we cannot distinguish a 14% lift from chance. Decision deferred to day 8 when we'll have 4,700 impressions per variant.'
choices.explain: Honest, specific, action-bound. This is what an honest framing looks like.

choices.label: 'B has shown a real, durable +6% lift over A across 22,000 impressions per variant; recommending we ship B.'
choices.explain: Specific lift, specific sample, specific recommendation. Defensible.

choices.label: 'B is performing better. We're confident.'
choices.explain: Confidence without sample size or lift band. Marketing astrology.

choices.label: 'Day 2 is showing strong B preference; rolling out tomorrow.'
choices.explain: The exact move the no-conclusion-yet rule was invented to prevent.

hi-IN.title: Naani ka tea-tasting test
hi-IN.md:
Naani chai banati hai do versions. Tu ek sip lekar bolta hai, "second one is better." Naani: "Beta, ek hi sip se kaise pata? Doosri ek bana ke do sip de." Tu repeat karta hai. Ab actually pata chalta hai.

A/B test bhi waisa hi hai. *Ek* sip — ek run — sample. Pattern dekhne ke liye tujhe enough volume chahiye. Naani always knew this. Marketing teams forgot.

en.title: The two-cup tea test
en.md: Your grandmother makes you taste two cups; you can't tell them apart on one sip. So you take three more from each. Now you can. Sample size is the only thing changing. Marketing dashboards forgot this; your grandmother didn't.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 47% lift at day 2, -3% at day 14
blocks.source: Anonymous performance marketer at a Bangalore D2C apparel brand
blocks.story:
Variant B was crushing it. Day 2: lift +47% over control. n=200 per arm. Manager said 'declare winner, scale to 100% traffic.' I caved.

Day 14 (post-rollout): aggregated lift over 30,000 users was -3%. We had taken 2 days of noise and called it signal. Worse: variant B was creative-fatigue-prone; lift decayed faster than control. **₹14 lakh of paid spend at -3% efficiency before we caught it.**

The minimum sample size for our ROAS variance was n≈4,700 per arm. Day 2 with n=200 had confidence interval of [-7%, +35%] — the +47% point estimate was within noise. I now run a power calculation BEFORE every test, write the minimum n on the test plan, and refuse to call winners before we hit it.
blocks.takeaway: Day-2 lift is almost always noise; minimum-sample-size discipline before declaring winners is non-negotiable.

blocks.title: Boss Battle: declare winner today?
blocks.setup: Sneha's running a creative A/B test on Meta. Day 2: variant B leading by 38% lift. Manager wants to scale to 100% traffic for Q2 push. Sneha has 30 minutes to decide.

points: Sample size is the unit of an A/B test, not days — measuring in days is confusing time with information.
The no-conclusion-yet rule: until you hit the pre-registered minimum sample, the answer to 'who's winning?' is no conclusion yet.
Every 'lift' has a noise band; if the lift is inside the band, the result is indistinguishable from chance.
Pre-registration binds your future self to honest decisions before you know the result; without it, you'll find a story for whatever happened.
If your campaign volume cannot deliver an honest sample within an honest timeframe, either pick a bigger lift to detect, or skip the test entirely.

lessons.title: Personalization Without Creepiness
lessons.subtitle: Segments, not individuals — and the would-you-tell-them test

blocks.md:
There are two stories about personalization. The vendor story: 'AI lets you treat every customer like a unique individual.' The reality: when you actually try, the cost goes up, the conversion ticks down, and a tenth of your audience unsubscribes the day they realise you saw them browse a sensitive product category at 11pm last Tuesday.

The lesson is not that personalization is bad. It's that the *unit* most marketing teams pick — the individual — is wrong. The unit that actually pays back is the **segment**: a few hundred to a few thousand customers who share a behavioural pattern. Segments scale; individuals don't. And segments don't trip the creepy-meter.

blocks.title: Mental model: segments not individuals
blocks.md:
True 1:1 personalization is a story marketing tools sell. In practice you almost never see it; what you see is **segment personalization disguised as individual personalization** — and when it actually drifts toward individual, customers notice and recoil.

The model: pick 4-8 behavioural segments, each big enough to be statistically meaningful (n > 200), and craft 4-8 distinct experiences. AI helps you ship them efficiently. But the unit is the segment, not the human.

Why: segments respect signal you have honestly earned (browsed kurtas, viewed checkout, tier-2 newcomer). Individuals tempt you to cross into signal you scraped. Segments scale; individuals creep.

hi-IN.title: Nykaa Q3 push — when personalization becomes creepy
hi-IN.md:
Imagine kar. Tu Nykaa pe kuch sensitive products dekha — anti-fungal cream, koi acne thing. Logout. Doosre din WhatsApp marketing message: "Hi Sneha, hope your skin journey is going well! Special discount on the items you were viewing yesterday."

Bhai. Yeh creepy hai. Item ka *naam* nahi liya, lekin pata chal gaya. Aur tu ne kabhi consent nahi diya WhatsApp pe yeh message paane ka.

Result: brand ke liye unsubscribe spike, social media pe screenshot, brand-trust permanent damage. Founder ne agency ko gaali di. Agency ne tool ko gaali di. Tool ne data-broker ko gaali di. Customer ne brand ko forever delete kar diya.

en.title: When personalization announces itself
en.md: A user browses a sensitive product category, logs out, and gets a WhatsApp message the next day mentioning the items they 'were viewing'. Even without naming the items, the moment of recognition — *they're watching me* — is what damages the brand. The customer didn't consent to that channel knowing that information.

blocks.caption: Watch (~30s) · Channel CAC across 6 quarters — arbitrage windows open and close.

blocks.md:
Not all signals are equal. The **consent ladder** ranks the data you might use, from highest trust to lowest. The rule: only use a signal if the user climbed *to* that rung; don't infer downward.

1. **Declared (top rung).** The user explicitly told you. 'I shop for festive wear.' 'I'm allergic to sulfates.' 'Send me Diwali offers.' Highest trust; near-zero creepy.
2. **Behavioural on your own surface.** They browsed kurtas twice last week, on your site, while logged in. Earned, declared by action.
3. **Aggregate cohort.** They share a pattern with 800 other customers — high cart-abandon rate after viewing accessories. Anonymised; safe.
4. **Inferred from third-party.** A data broker says they're in 'household income tier 3'. *Below* the consent floor; don't use.
5. **Cross-device fingerprinting / non-consented enrichment.** Same answer. Don't.

The ladder doesn't say AI is bad at personalization. It says: AI *should only operate on signals that climbed the ladder honestly*. Most personalization disasters happen because someone fed AI signals from rungs 4 or 5 and called it 'smart'.

steps.label: Step 1 — List the signals you have
steps.body: Inventory: declared preferences, on-site behaviour, purchase history, channel engagement. Don't reach for inferred or third-party signals yet.

steps.label: Step 2 — Filter by ladder rung
steps.body: Drop everything below rung 3 (cohort). What remains is your honest signal pool.

steps.label: Step 3 — Group into 4-8 segments
steps.body: Each segment: n > 200 customers, behaviourally distinct, paired with a clear hypothesis ('cart abandoners after accessories view → respond to social proof').

steps.label: Step 4 — Craft segment-level content
steps.body: AI drafts 4-8 versions, one per segment. Voice anchor applied. 3-pass review.

steps.label: Step 5 — Set a creepy-meter check
steps.body: Final pass: 'If we showed this email to the customer with the line attached: "we sent this because you did X", would they nod or recoil?' If recoil, scale back the signal.

blocks.prompt: Your team has access to: declared preferences (rung 1), on-site browsing (rung 2), purchase history (rung 1-2), and a third-party data enrichment service (rung 4). Which combination should AI personalization actually use?

choices.label: Declared preferences + on-site browsing + purchase history. Skip the third-party enrichment.
choices.explain: Right. Stay above the consent floor. The first three are signals the customer earned for you; the third-party data is signals you bought without their consent.

choices.label: All four — more signal is more accuracy.
choices.explain: More signal isn't more accuracy when the extra signal is non-consented. It's more risk.

choices.label: Just declared preferences; everything else is inference.
choices.explain: Too restrictive. On-site behaviour is a signal the customer gave you on your surface; using it is fair.

choices.label: Just the third-party enrichment; it's the most powerful predictor.
choices.explain: Powerful and creepy aren't the same as good. The third-party data fails the consent ladder.

hi-IN.title: Mehmaan ka rule
hi-IN.md:
Mehmaan tere ghar aata hai. Tu unka pasandida chai banata hai *kyunki unhone bola tha pehle*. Achha. Warm.

Lekin agar tu unke fridge mein peep maar ke pata laga le ki unhe oat milk pasand hai, aur uska use kare — woh creepy hai. Even though information same hai.

Declared signal vs inferred signal ka pura difference yeh hai. Mehmaan ne kya bola, vs tu ne kya jasoosi ki.

en.title: The guest rule
en.md: When a guest tells you their tea preference, using it is hospitality. When you peek in their fridge to find out, using it is creepy. The information is the same; the consent path is different. Personalization works the same way. Use what they told you. Don't use what you snooped.

blocks.md:
The simplest creepy-meter check is also the most honest one: **for every personalised piece, write the line you'd say if the customer asked 'how did you know?' If you can say it without flinching, you're fine. If you'd want to dodge, you're over the line.**

Three examples:

- 'You favourited this kurta last week, so we wanted to let you know it's back in stock.' — *would say.* The customer earned that signal by clicking favourite.
- 'You browsed accessories twice in the last 14 days, so here's a 10% discount.' — *would say, with light squirm.* The signal is on-site, behaviour-based, and the discount is a fair offer. Acceptable.
- 'Your household income tier suggests you'd like our premium range.' — *would not say.* No customer ever consented to be classified that way. The discomfort of saying it is the test failing.

Most teams skip the test because it adds friction. The friction is the feature. It's the thing that stops you from shipping the email that gets you on the front page of a privacy story.

scenarios.situation: User favourited a kurta. Two weeks later: 'Hi! That kurta is back in stock; here's a 5% loyalty offer.'
scenarios.explain: Declared action (favourite). Honest signal. Mild offer. The line 'you favourited it' lands fine.

scenarios.situation: User browsed 6 product pages over 3 sessions, didn't buy. Email: 'Looks like you've been comparing options — here are 3 user reviews of the most-viewed item.'
scenarios.explain: Behavioural signal on your site is fair, but 'comparing options' announces surveillance more than the signal warrants. Soften the line, ship.

scenarios.situation: Customer's WhatsApp number wasn't given for marketing. Marketing tool sends them a Diwali offer 'because they're in your database'.
scenarios.explain: WhatsApp without explicit channel consent is the regulated landmine. India's DPDPA enforces this; not a brand judgement call, a legal one.

scenarios.situation: Email: 'Based on your previous purchases (last 12 months: kids' clothing 4x), here's our new kids' collection.'
scenarios.explain: Purchase history is a rung-1/2 signal, transparently named. The line 'you've bought from this category' is comfortable to say out loud.

scenarios.situation: Push notification 'You spent ₹2,400 on us last quarter — top 5% customer! Special offer'
scenarios.explain: Purchase history is fine. Tier-ranking ('top 5%') is starting to creep — implies a behind-the-scenes scoring the customer didn't agree to. Reframe ('thank you for being a regular customer'), ship.

scenarios.situation: Email: 'We noticed you visited from Pune; here's a Tier-2 starter kit.' (User is a logged-in customer who never declared their city.)
scenarios.explain: Geolocation from IP without declared address is over the consent line. Even if technically possible, the line 'we tracked your IP' fails the test.

blocks.title: The classic trap: creepy 1:1 personalization that backfires
blocks.md:
The trap is seductive because vendors sell it as the dream: 'AI lets you treat every customer like an individual.' What this becomes in practice is an email pipeline trained on every signal you can scrape, regulated and unregulated, until one of them shows up in a customer's inbox in a way they didn't expect.

The failure is non-linear. 95% of customers don't notice. 4% notice and unsubscribe quietly. 1% notice, screenshot, and post. That 1% is enough. India's DPDPA in 2026 has teeth; the social cost is bigger than the legal one.

The defence is upstream: don't operate below the consent floor in the first place. Segment-level personalization on declared and on-site signals doesn't trip the wire.

blocks.instruction:
You're designing a Diwali campaign for a Pune D2C brand expanding into Tier-2 cities. Available signals: declared festive preferences (rung 1), on-site browsing of festive collection (rung 2), 12-month purchase history (rung 1-2), pin code from delivery address (rung 1, declared at checkout), inferred lifestyle persona from a third-party data partner (rung 4).

Design 4 segments. For each, write:
- The signal(s) you'd use (and why you skipped any)
- The 'we sent this because…' line
- Whether it passes the would-you-tell-them test
blocks.expected:
Skipped: third-party lifestyle persona (rung 4). Below the consent floor.

Segment 1 — Festive shoppers, declared
- Signals: declared festive preference + on-site browse this season.
- Line: 'We sent this because you told us festive collections matter to you, and you've been browsing this season's drop.'
- Passes the test cleanly.

Segment 2 — Tier-2 newcomers (first-time, this quarter, pin code outside top 8 cities)
- Signals: pin code (declared at checkout) + first-purchase status.
- Line: 'Thank you for being one of our newer customers; here's a Tier-2 starter kit with regional shipping.'
- Passes — pin code was declared, framing is welcoming.

Segment 3 — Repeat 3+ purchasers in the last year
- Signals: purchase history.
- Line: 'You've shopped with us multiple times this year; here's a thank-you offer on your usual category.'
- Passes — purchase history is the cleanest signal.

Segment 4 — Cart-abandoners after viewing festive collection
- Signals: on-site cart and view behaviour.
- Line: 'You added this kurta to your cart but didn't check out — Diwali stock is moving fast; here's free shipping.'
- Borderline-passes; would soften 'we noticed you didn't check out' into 'in case you're still deciding'.

blocks.prompt: An AI-personalization vendor offers to enrich your customer base with 'lifestyle-based household income tiers' for ₹3 per record. Your customer base is 200,000. Which of these are honest reasons to refuse? (pick two)

choices.label: The signal lives below the consent floor; using it fails the would-you-tell-them test.
choices.explain: Right. The customer never consented to be income-classified by a third party for marketing.

choices.label: Under DPDPA-style regulations, third-party enrichment without explicit consent is a regulated and increasingly enforced risk.
choices.explain: Right. By 2026 the legal teeth are real; the optionality has shrunk.

choices.label: ₹6 lakh is too expensive for what it would deliver.
choices.explain: Cost objection is weak; it sidesteps the substantive issue. Even at ₹0 it would be wrong to use.

choices.label: AI personalization doesn't work.
choices.explain: Sweeping and false. The objection is to *this signal*, not all personalization.

hi-IN.title: Naani aur shaadi-fixing aunty
hi-IN.md:
Naani biodata padhke shaadi fix karti thi — explicit information. Caste, salary, height, family. Sab declared. Awkward, but consensual.

Shaadi-fixing aunty thi jo padosi se 'pucha-pacha' ke information jutati thi. "Suni hai unka beta US mein kaam karta hai..." Yeh inferred. Yeh creepy. Yeh aaj DPDPA violation banti.

Marketing personalization ka choice waisa hi hai. Tu Naani-mode mein chal sakta hai. Tu aunty-mode mein chal sakta hai. Aunty-mode mein customer ek baar pakad le toh forever damage.

en.title: The biodata vs the aunty network
en.md: Two ways the previous generation gathered information for arranged marriages: declared biodata or the gossip-aunty network. The first was awkward but consensual; the second was inferred from sources nobody had agreed to. Marketing personalization has the same choice. Pick biodata-mode.

blocks.title: Field Notes: 'we noticed you spent 47 minutes on the kurta page'
blocks.source: Anonymous CMO at a Mumbai apparel D2C, 4-year-old brand
blocks.story:
Our personalization vendor pitched us '1:1 personalization at scale.' We piloted on 47,000 high-LTV customers. The hero email said: *'Hi Priya, we noticed you spent 47 minutes on the kurta-with-dupatta page on Tuesday at 9 PM...'*

Response: 23% spam-flag rate (industry avg: 0.3%). 14 customers contacted support saying they 'felt watched.' Twitter picked it up. **Brand-trust score dropped 18 points.** Took 2 quarters to recover.

We shifted to segment-based: 'hi from your favorite kurta brand — based on your recent visits, here are 3 you might like.' Same intent, no creep. Click-through went UP from baseline. Spam-flag back to 0.3%.

The lesson wasn't 'personalization is bad.' It was 'showing the user that you watched them is bad'. Segments hide that the watching is happening; 1:1 advertises it.
blocks.takeaway: Segments are personalization that doesn't advertise the surveillance. 1:1 specifics in customer-facing copy are a trust trap.

points: Personalize at the segment level, not the individual level — segments scale, individuals creep.
The consent ladder ranks signals by trust earned; never operate below the consent floor (third-party enrichment, fingerprinting).
The would-you-tell-them test is the cheapest creepy-meter you have: if you'd flinch saying the 'we sent this because…' line, redesign.
Most personalization disasters come from feeding AI signals it shouldn't have access to, not from AI itself.
By 2026, India's DPDPA is teeth-bearing; brand cost of a privacy story is bigger than the legal cost, and both are real.

audioChapters.label: Move 2 — The kill criterion that holds

blocks.md:
Open any marketing dashboard in 2026 and you'll find 47 widgets, 9 filters, 3 sparkline rails. Reach. Engagement. Sentiment. Brand recall index. Share-of-voice quintiles. The dashboard cost ₹4.5 lakh to commission and is updated nightly by an AI pipeline.

The founder looks at it once a week, says 'looks healthy', and goes back to worrying about cash. Nobody, including you, can name the *one* number that would make you kill a campaign tomorrow if it dropped 25%.

That is a vanity dashboard. It feels like measurement. It is decoration. The fix is not 'better dashboard'; the fix is *fewer numbers, attached to actions, attached to deadlines*. This lesson is the discipline.

blocks.title: Mental model: one north-star, attached to an action
blocks.md:
A real north-star metric has three properties:

1. **It maps to economic outcome.** Not awareness, not engagement; revenue, margin, retention, or payback.
2. **It changes slowly enough to mean something, fast enough to drive a decision.** Daily revenue is too noisy; quarterly retention is too slow. 14-90 day metrics are usually the sweet spot.
3. **It has a kill threshold and a scale threshold *in writing, before launch*.** 'If north-star drops below X by day Z, we kill. If above Y, we scale.'

Without #3, you don't have a metric. You have decoration.

For most Indian D2C brands, the cleanest north-stars are: **90-day repeat purchase rate**, **6-month contribution margin per customer**, or **paid-CAC payback in days**. Pick one. Demote the rest to supporting cast.

en.title: The 'how much did you actually save' test
en.md: When you brag about a 60% discount on a phone you didn't need, your mom asks how much you actually saved versus your old working phone. She's asking for the north-star metric. The 60% off is a vanity headline. The two-question discipline of 'compared to what?' and 'attached to what action?' is what separates measurement from theatre.

blocks.md:
The right cadence for marketing iteration in 2026 is 14 days. Not weekly (too noisy, churns the team), not quarterly (too slow, kills agility). 14 days is enough sample to make honest calls and short enough to not bleed money on bad ideas.

The loop has four beats:

1. **Day 0 (Launch day).** Pre-register the campaign: target audience, channels, expected CAC and ROAS, *the kill criterion*, and the scale criterion. This is a one-pager. If it takes more than an hour to write, your scope is too big.
2. **Day 7 (Mid-loop check).** Look at the data; do not act on it. (Sample size is usually still inside the noise band on day 7.) Note any directional signal. Do not pivot.
3. **Day 10 (The hard date).** This is the kill-criterion checkpoint. If north-star is below the kill threshold, you stop. Even if you have a good story for why. *Especially* if you have a good story for why.
4. **Day 14 (Decide).** Scale, kill, or extend. Each option has a specific spend implication. Document the decision and the reason.

Why day 10 instead of day 14 for the kill check? Because the cost of running a losing campaign for 4 extra days is real money, and 'just give it more time' is the most common excuse for letting a kill criterion decay. The hard date is the discipline.

steps.label: Day 0 — Pre-register
steps.body: Launch AI-drafted Meta ads against current human-written control. Target: ₹40k spend per arm. North-star metric: paid-CAC over 14 days. Kill criterion: 'If by day 10, AI arm CAC is > ₹1,200 (current control is ₹847), we kill.' Scale: 'If AI arm CAC is < ₹720 by day 14 with n>4,000 conversions, we shift 60% of budget.'

steps.label: Day 7 — Look
steps.body: AI arm CAC at day 7: ₹980 (n=820 conversions). Control: ₹860. Note: AI is trending up but sample inside noise band. Don't act. Continue.

steps.label: Day 10 — Kill check
steps.body: AI arm CAC: ₹1,090 (n=1,400). Below the kill threshold of ₹1,200, but only barely. Continue running by the rule. Note: temptation to kill early ('it's clearly trending bad') is also an unauthorized override of the rule. Honor the threshold.

steps.label: Day 14 — Decide
steps.body: AI arm CAC: ₹1,140 (n=2,200). Control: ₹880. Result: AI arm is worse, but not catastrophically so. Decision: kill the AI arm; document the learning ('AI ads underperform our anchored human voice for this audience at this stage'); rerun the test on a different funnel stage where stakes per piece are lower.

steps.label: Wrap — Decision Doc
steps.body: Write the one-paragraph 'what we learned' note. Without it, the loop is just churn. With it, the team has a memory and the next experiment is sharper.

blocks.prompt: Day 11 of a campaign. North-star metric is just barely below the kill threshold. The team argues 'it's only 4 days from end; let it run'. The honest call is:

choices.label: Honor the kill criterion. The threshold existed precisely for the moment when you don't like the answer.
choices.explain: Right. A criterion you only honor when it confirms what you wanted is a wish, not a criterion. Kill at the threshold.

choices.label: Extend to day 14; maybe it recovers.
choices.explain: This is how kill criteria die — the death-by-extension mode. Document and avoid.

choices.label: Increase budget to lower CAC.
choices.explain: Doubling down on a campaign that's missing the target is the failure mode the criterion was designed to stop.

choices.label: Switch attribution windows until the metric looks fine.
choices.explain: Attribution-window p-hacking. The most expensive way to lie to yourself.

Day 11. AI ad campaign band karne ka time hai. Founder Slack pe: "Yaar, 14 din chhoti window hai. Long-term branding mein aisi cheezein 60-90 din mein dikhti hain. Continue karte hain."

Bhai. Wahi founder day 5 par kya bola tha? "Yeh kaam kyun nahi kar raha?" Same campaign. Same data. Same person. Sirf direction badal gayi.

Kill criterion exactly is liye written hota hai launch se pehle. Ki day 11 par tu apne aap se argue na kare. Tu ne pehle written kiya tha — "day 10, CAC > ₹1,200, kill." Day 10 aaya. Threshold cross hua. Kill hai. Aur kuch nahi.

en.title: The day-11 'we need more time' move
en.md: On day 5 the founder asks why the campaign isn't working. On day 11 the same founder asks for 'more time to let branding compound'. Same campaign, same data, mood-driven framing. The kill criterion is written before launch precisely so day-11 you can't argue with day-0 you. Honor what you wrote.

blocks.text: Move 2 — The kill criterion that holds

blocks.md:
A kill criterion that survives Friday night at 11pm has four properties:

1. **Pre-registered.** Written before launch, sent to the team, dated.
2. **Specific.** A number, a date, a metric. Not 'we'll know it when we see it'.
3. **Cheap to honor.** Killing should be a single Slack message and an ad pause, not a five-meeting deliberation.
4. **Pre-emptively immune to the three excuses.**

The three excuses are nearly universal:

- *'Give it more time.'* — Cure: write into the criterion *what would actually change* with more time. If you can't name a structural reason, more time is just hope.
- *'The creative just needs a tweak.'* — Cure: pre-commit that creative tweaks are a *new* test (with its own kill criterion), not an extension of this one.
- *'The comparison window is wrong; let's switch to last-touch / first-touch / view-through.'* — Cure: lock the attribution model in writing on day 0. Switching mid-test is p-hacking.

The written kill criterion looks like this for the Pune wellness brand:

> *'If by day 10 of the AI-ads test, paid CAC is above ₹1,200 (vs control's ₹847), we will pause the test. We will not extend, we will not retune creative, and we will not switch from last-click to view-through attribution. The test ends; we document; the next experiment is on a different stage of the funnel.'*

Three sentences. The team can hold it. The founder can argue with it on day 11, but the criterion will win, because the criterion was right when both of them agreed.

coach.role: D2C veteran, has killed 23 campaigns at the threshold and saved roughly ₹1.6 crore by doing it

intro: Last round. I'll give you six day-10 checkpoints. You tell me: **kill**, **continue**, or **escalate** (founder/team needs to decide).
The pre-registered kill criterion is what guides you. Don't import new logic on the fly.
Easy to be hard before launch. Hard to be hard at 11pm. We practice for the second one.

scenarios.situation: Pre-registered: 'Kill if CAC > ₹1,200 by day 10.' Day 10: CAC = ₹1,340. Founder: 'It's only 4 days from end.'
scenarios.explain: Kill. The criterion was clear. Day-11-founder doesn't override day-0 founder. This is the canonical kill case.

scenarios.situation: Pre-registered: 'Kill if ROAS < 2.5 by day 10.' Day 10: ROAS = 2.6. Performance marketer: 'Trending down; let's pull the plug now.'
scenarios.explain: Continue. ROAS is *above* the threshold. Pulling the plug now imports new logic mid-test. The criterion is the criterion both ways.

scenarios.situation: Pre-registered: 'Kill if conversion rate < 1.8% by day 10.' Day 10: conversion = 1.7% — but a national-news event two days ago temporarily depressed all e-commerce by ~12% measured industry-wide.
scenarios.explain: Escalate. The criterion is breached, but a documented external shock affected all numbers. Bring the data to the team and decide explicitly whether to kill or extend by 5 days. Document the override; don't make it silent.

scenarios.situation: Pre-registered: 'Kill if north-star (90-day repeat purchase) is on pace below 22% by day 10.' Day 10: pace = 19%.
scenarios.explain: Kill. Pace metrics are valid criteria; honor them. The 90-day full data won't arrive in time to save the campaign; the leading indicator is what you committed to.

scenarios.situation: No pre-registered criterion was written. Day 10: CAC has crept from ₹780 to ₹990. Team is split.
scenarios.explain: Escalate. Without a criterion you literally cannot kill or continue 'by the rules'. Use this as the moment to write a criterion *now* for the remaining four days, get team sign-off, and then honor it. Document the gap so it doesn't happen next time.

scenarios.situation: Pre-registered: 'Kill if CAC > ₹1,200 by day 10.' Day 10: CAC = ₹1,180. Founder: 'It's basically there; let's kill anyway.'
scenarios.explain: Continue. CAC is *below* the kill threshold; killing now is again importing new logic. The whole point is that day-0 you and day-10 you have to agree only on the threshold, not on the call. The threshold spoke; you continue.

blocks.title: The classic trap: vanity metrics dashboard
blocks.md:
The trap is identifiable in a sentence: **a dashboard is a vanity dashboard if no number on it has a kill threshold attached.** Every metric without a threshold is decoration. The dashboard might look beautiful, cost money, and update nightly via an AI pipeline; without thresholds, it cannot drive a single decision.

The cure is brutal subtraction. Take the dashboard. For each widget, ask 'what number on this widget would make us kill or scale a campaign?' If the answer is 'we'd discuss it', the widget gets demoted to an FYI tab. The main view holds only metrics with attached actions. You will end up with 3-6 numbers. That is correct. That is the point.

blocks.instruction:
You're launching a 14-day Meta-ads test for a Coimbatore-based D2C brand. Current paid CAC: ₹847. LTV: ₹4,200. Test variant: AI-generated dynamic creative against current human-written control. Daily impressions per variant: 2,000.

Write the day-0 pre-registration document. Cover:
- North-star metric and why
- Specific kill criterion (number + date)
- Specific scale criterion (number + date)
- Attribution model (lock it now)
- The three excuses you anticipate, and the pre-emption for each

Max one page.
blocks.expected:
Pre-Registration: AI-Ads Test, 14-Day Loop

North-star: Paid CAC over 14 days, last-click attribution, fully loaded (ad spend / new acquired customers).

Kill criterion (day 10): If AI variant CAC is > ₹1,150 at day 10, with n > 1,200 conversions, we pause the AI variant. (Threshold = current control ₹847 + 35% buffer; below this we are not learning anything actionable.)

Scale criterion (day 14): If AI variant CAC is < ₹720 with n > 4,000 conversions, we shift 50% of next month's budget to AI dynamic creative.

Attribution: Last-click on the platform's reported window. Locked. We will not switch to view-through, multi-touch, or first-click during this test.

Pre-empted excuses:
- 'Give it more time.' — No. The 14-day window is the answer; there is no structural reason a campaign that fails day-10 would recover by day-14.
- 'Creative just needs a tweak.' — Tweaks are a new test, with its own pre-registration. Mid-flight tuning is excluded.
- 'Comparison window is wrong.' — The window was chosen on day 0 with team sign-off. Locked.

Signed: [name], [date].
